newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Digital TV dispute highlights pay-TV problem.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Digital TV dispute highlights pay-TV problem.

text.p: A row over digital television in Spain highlights a dilemma that has dogged efforts to introduce the new TV services across Europe: what is the best way to control access to pay programmes?

All parties concerned say they want to ensure that consumers need only one decoder to receive the digital signals that will connect them to hundreds of high-quality channels and interactive services such as home banking and shopping.
But they differ over the best technology for achieving that goal.

The European Commission, after several warnings, threatened in July to take the Spanish government to court for imposing a solution that favours a technology known as "multicrypt" -- the second time the EU executive has intervened in a national battle over decoders.
The move was welcomed by many pay-TV broadcasters, who agree with the Commission that the Spanish law illegally restricts free trade within the Union.

"The clear choice made by the Spanish government in favour of one specific technology, as well as the obligation to obtain prior authorisation for its use, is contrary to the rules which should obtain in the single market," the Association of Commercial Television in Europe told the Commission in a letter.

But public broadcasters are less enthusiastic, fearing that their commercial rivals are promoting simulcrypt -- a proprietary system -- in an attempt to maintain control over decoder technology at the expense of a unified, open market.

"History shows how open markets and open systems like GSM, the digital mobile telephone system, make sense for industry and the public," the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) said in a recent policy paper.
CONTROVERSY INVOLVES "CONDITIONAL ACCESS" SYSTEMS
The controversy concerns "conditional access" systems -- the technology used in decoders, or "set-top boxes," to ensure that only paying viewers receive encrypted programmes.

While digital TV technology in Europe has been largely standardised by an industry-government group known as the Digital Video Broadcasting (DVB) Project, established pay TV operators such as British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc and Canal Plus have insisted on keeping control over their conditional access systems.
They argue that a single set of standards could lead to piracy on a vast scale because digital thieves would have only one technology to crack across Europe.
"When you make a safe, you don't publish the shape of the key," said Erik Lambert, adviser to the CEO of Canal Plus.

The DVB agreed instead to draw up specifications for a "common interface" that manufacturers could install on a voluntary basis, allowing consumers to insert conditional access modules from different broadcasters into their decoders.

It also drew up a code of conduct to govern use of the "simulcrypt" technology, which allows broadcasters to maintain control over their own decoders but to negotiate agreements allowing rivals to transmit programmes through them.
The EU, wary of intervening too heavily in the fledgling market, declined to impose a conditional access system when it adopted rules on transmission signals for digital TV in 1995.
But it said broadcasters must allow rivals to transmit programmes through their decoders on a non-discriminatory basis.
In Spain, the row began when two big digital TV operators opted for different technologies for their decoders.
Via Digital, which plans to launch a 35-channel basic digital pay TV package in September, plans to offer multicrypt decoders that work with a common interface.
CanalSatelite, led by Canal Plus, is already on the market with decoders using the simulcrypt system.
The Spanish law that has been challenged by the Commission asks operators to provide compatible decoders to ensure that consumers need to buy only one set-top box.

But it says that in the absence of an accord between companies, the multicrypt system must be adopted, prompting allegations that the government was favouring Via Digital, an alliance that includes telecoms operator Telefonica de Espana and state television RTVE.

Each side says its choice will benefit the consumer. "I only know that we will start to operate in September with our decoder, which is universal, meaning that anyone who buys it can access our offer or any other offer presented," Via Digital chairman Pedro Perez Fernandez told a news conference in July.

Canal Plus argues, however, that the multicrypt system is cumbersome for consumers since they have to insert a new module every time they switch broadcasters -- or buy a more expensive box that includes space for multiple modules.
"Simulcrypt puts the cost and complexity at the digital broadcaster's end," Lambert said.
THE COMMISSION INTERVENES FOR A SECOND TIME
The Commission's threat to take Spain before the European Court of Justice marks the second time the EU executive has intervened in a national battle over digital decoders.
Just over a year ago, it called European broadcasters together in an effort to defuse a battle that had produced rival decoder technologies in Germany.
Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann said then that the Commission did not want to see fragmented markets with consumers forced to invest in more than one box.

The German market has since sorted itself out, with media giants Bertelsmann AG and the Kirch Group both agreeing to use Kirch's "d-box" decoder technology. But the issue has still not been resolved at EU level.

To complicate matters, most EU countries have not yet implemented the 1995 EU directive on transmission standards. Therefore, the Commission has not prepared a report on market developments in the sector that the directive said should be submitted by July 1, 1997.

The EBU was hoping that review would address issues such as conditional access systems and the "language" used to transmit the electronic programme guides that will guide consumers around the digital TV world. But the Commission says its priority is to get the original rules turned into national law.
"That's our preoccupation, to get it done and get it done correctly," one official said.

The European Association of Consumer Electronics Manufacturers (EACEM) is concerned that the Commission's inaction will lead to market fragmentation. "EACEM's position is that we need some more standardisation on what's happening," said Rony Van Haegenberg, the group's technical director.
While sometimes the market works best without interference, "in the case of digital television, I would suspect it's not going to be very efficient," he added.
